section.title: The Two Beasts
section.sectionRationale: This chapter is the dragon's answer to his own defeat in chapter 12. Unable to destroy the woman and her offspring directly, he raises up two proxies: a beast from the sea who wields blasphemous imperial power, and a beast from the earth who compels worship of the first beast through deceptive signs and economic coercion. The unit holds together as the full unveiling of the dragon's unholy counterfeit trinity, dragon, beast, and false prophet, before the vision of the Lamb and His people in chapter 14 directly answers it.
section.thesis: The dragon rules through two beasts, one that wields blasphemous political power and wins the world's worship by imitating a resurrection, and one that enforces that worship through deceptive signs and economic coercion, so that every person, marked or unmarked, is forced to choose whom they will serve.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the beast from the sea and its blasphemous authority; the beast's war on the saints and the call to perseverance; the beast from the earth, the false prophet who deceives with signs; and the mark of the beast, its name, and the number 666.

verses.text: Then I saw a {{therion|beast}} with ten horns and seven heads rising out of the sea. There were ten royal crowns on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads.
The beast I saw was like a leopard, with the feet of a bear and the mouth of a lion. And the dragon gave the beast his power and his throne and great authority.
One of the heads of the beast appeared to be mortally wounded. But the mortal wound was healed, and the whole world marveled and followed the beast.
They {{proskyneo|worshiped}} the dragon who had given authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?”

units.label: War on the saints, and the call to endure
units.note: a limited authority, an unlimited demand

verses.text: The beast was given a mouth to speak arrogant and blasphemous words, and authority to act for 42 months.
And the beast opened its mouth to speak blasphemies against God and to slander His name and His tabernacle, those who dwell in heaven.
Then the beast was permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them, and it was given authority over every tribe and people and tongue and nation.
And all who dwell on the earth will worship the beast, all whose names have not been written from the foundation of the world in the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain.
He who has an ear, let him hear:

“If anyone is destined for captivity, into captivity he will go; if anyone is to die by the sword, by the sword he must be killed.” Here is a call for the {{hypomone|perseverance}} and faith of the saints.

units.label: The beast from the earth
units.note: the false prophet who deceives with signs

verses.text: Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. This beast had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon.
And this beast exercised all the authority of the first beast and caused the earth and those who dwell in it to worship the first beast, whose mortal wound had been healed.
And the second beast performed great signs to cause even fire from heaven to come down to earth in the presence of the people.

Because of the signs it was given to perform on behalf of the first beast, it deceived those who dwell on the earth, telling them to make an image to the beast that had been wounded by the sword and yet had lived.
The second beast was permitted to give breath to the image of the first beast, so that the image could speak and cause all who refused to worship it to be killed.

units.label: The mark, the name, and the number
units.note: economic coercion and a call for wisdom

verses.text: And the second beast required all people small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, to receive a {{charagma|mark}} on their right hand or on their forehead,
so that no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark, the name of the beast or the number of its name.
Here is a call for wisdom: Let the one who has insight calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and that number is 666.

therion.gloss: A wild beast, a monster. John draws its features, leopard, bear, and lion, straight from Daniel's four beasts, now combined into one final, composite empire. The word marks the beast as an animal in nature, however human its face, a creature of appetite and violence set against the Lamb who was slain.

proskyneo.gloss: To worship, to fall down and pay homage. It is the same word used throughout Revelation for the worship owed to God and the Lamb alone; here the whole world bows it to the dragon and the beast instead, the counterfeit of true worship at the heart of the chapter.

charagma.gloss: A mark, stamp, or engraved brand, used of the imperial seal on official documents and of brands on slaves or soldiers. The beast's charagma on hand and forehead parodies the seal of the living God placed on His servants' foreheads in chapter 7, forcing visible allegiance into the ordinary business of daily life.

hypomone.gloss: Steadfast endurance, perseverance under pressure rather than passive waiting. It is the quality repeatedly called for as the saints face the beast's authority to conquer them; it does not mean escaping suffering but remaining faithful through it, after the pattern of the Lamb who was slain.

basic.context: Chapter 12 ended with the dragon defeated in heaven but furious on earth. Now he raises two agents: a beast from the sea that combines the horror of Daniel's four beasts and wields the dragon's own power, and a beast from the earth that works miracles to force the world to worship the first beast. Together they demand worship and control commerce through a mark, so that no one can buy or sell without declaring allegiance.
basic.hermeneutics: Readers debate exactly who or what the beast and its number, 666, pointed to first, whether a Roman emperor like Nero or Domitian, a future end-time ruler, or a recurring pattern of God-defying power in every age. The chapter itself does not require solving that puzzle to be understood: it is meant to unmask worldly power and false religion as the dragon's instruments and to call suffering believers to discernment and perseverance rather than compromise.
basic.originalLanguages: The therion, the beast, is an animal at heart however impressive its crowns. The world offers it proskyneo, worship, that belongs to God alone. It brands its followers with a charagma, a mark, on hand or forehead, a counterfeit of God's own seal. And in the face of its authority, the saints are called to hypomone, steady endurance, and faith.
basic.typology: The beast's healed mortal wound apes the true death and resurrection of the Lamb, a counterfeit miracle for a counterfeit king. Daniel's four beasts, lion, bear, leopard, and a terrifying fourth, are gathered into this one final beast, showing that every proud empire in history was a preview of this last, blasphemous power.
basic.christ: Against the beast's fake resurrection stands the Lamb who was truly slain and truly lives, and it is His Book of Life, not the beast's mark, that secures a person's name. The call to endurance echoes Christ's own patient suffering, and it is by trusting Him, not by military resistance, that the saints are told to face the beast.
basic.god: God's sovereignty frames the whole chapter: the beast is repeatedly said to be given, permitted, allowed to act, and for a limited time, 42 months, not forever. However fierce the beast, it operates only within boundaries God Himself sets, and the outcome is already decided in the Book of Life kept from the foundation of the world.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 7:2-7 supplies the beast's composite features. Revelation 7:2-3 shows God's own seal on His servants' foreheads, the pattern the beast's mark counterfeits. Revelation 12:9 and 17 explain the dragon's fury behind both beasts. And Revelation 20:10 shows the beast and false prophet finally and fully judged.
basic.oneStory: From the serpent in Eden to the beasts of Daniel to this final beast, one enemy keeps raising counterfeit power to demand the worship due to God alone. The Bible's answer is consistent: the slain and risen Lamb, whose Book of Life secures His people against every empire, mark, and counterfeit miracle the dragon can produce.

context.literary:
Revelation 13 follows directly from the last sentence of chapter 12, where the dragon takes his stand on the sand of the sea. The beast that rises from that sea is his answer to defeat. The chapter has two halves of almost equal length, the sea beast in verses 1 to 10 and the earth beast in verses 11 to 18, and each half ends with a call to the reader: 'He who has an ear, let him hear,' with the summons to endurance, verses 9 and 10, and 'Here is a call for wisdom,' verse 18. The phrase about having an ear has not been heard since the letters to the churches, Revelation 3:22, so the reader is reminded that this is a word to the churches.

The chapter is built on imitation. The dragon gives the beast his power, throne, and authority, verse 2, as the Father gave the Son authority. The beast has a mortal wound that was healed, which parodies the slain Lamb. The crowd asks, 'Who is like the beast?' mimicking the praise of God. The second beast has two horns like a lamb but speaks like the dragon, so it passes for gentle while carrying the dragon's voice. The counterfeit is the chapter's main literary device, and every feature that seems to belong to God is shown in a distorted form.

The repeated 'was given' marks a second theme. The beast is given a mouth, authority, permission to wage war. The beast is not self-made, and its power is always on loan.
context.historical:
The Roman world was full of the language John borrows. Cities in Asia Minor competed for the honor of building temples to the emperor, and the churches John addresses lived among them. Titles like 'lord' and 'god' and the Greek title Sebastos, meaning 'worthy of reverence,' were attached to the ruler, and the cult of the emperor tied loyalty to the state to ritual worship. Refusing the rites could bring suspicion and loss. Trade guilds also held feasts in honor of their patron gods and sometimes the emperor, which is part of the background of the troubles at Pergamum and Thyatira in Revelation 2 and 3, and it helps explain why the second beast's control of buying and selling, verse 17, would be felt in daily work.

The sea beast is built from the animals of Daniel 7:3 to 7, where four beasts arise from the sea as four kingdoms, and Daniel's fourth beast has ten horns. John reverses the order: leopard, bear, lion. Some first-century readers believed that Nero, who died in AD 68, would return, and the legend of Nero redivivus is often connected to the healed head. In Hebrew letters, the name Nero Caesar adds up to 666, and a spelling without the final letter gives 616, which is the variant mentioned in the BSB footnote. The Greek letters and the Hebrew letters both served as numbers, so a riddle in numbers was a familiar kind of puzzle.
context.canonical:
Chapter 13 gathers many strands from Scripture's long history of tyrant powers. Daniel 7 is the main source, but the horn's arrogant words and the limited season of its power echo Daniel 7:8, 7:25, and 11:36. The golden image that all had to worship on pain of death, Daniel 3:1 to 6, is the pattern for the image of verses 14 and 15. The false prophets who give signs and wonders to lead people after other gods, Deuteronomy 13:1 to 3, are the model for the earth beast, and Jesus warned of false messiahs and false prophets who would perform great signs, Matthew 24:24. Paul describes the lawless one who sits in God's temple, displaying himself as God, with the work of Satan and counterfeit signs, 2 Thessalonians 2:3 to 10, and John mentions the antichrist already at work, 1 John 2:18.

The sea beast parodies the Lamb of chapter 5, who was slain, and the earth beast later appears as the false prophet, Revelation 16:13, 19:20, and 20:10. The mark on the hand and forehead recalls Deuteronomy 6:8, where Israel binds God's words on the hand and between the eyes, and the seal on the foreheads of God's servants, Revelation 7:3.

Romans 13:1 to 7 sees the state as God's servant, 1 Peter 2:13 to 17 honors the emperor, and Revelation 13 shows what the state becomes when it claims what belongs to God.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wanted his readers to see through the glamour of power. A world that marveled at the beast and asked who could fight it would have made loyalty to Christ look foolish. John's account shows what lies beneath: a power given by the dragon, allowed for a limited time, and aimed at demanding worship that belongs to God alone. He did not ask the churches to be afraid; he asked them to be clear-eyed.

He also meant to shape the church's response. The call in verse 10 is not for armed resistance or for withdrawal but for 'perseverance and faith.' The saints are warned that captivity and death are coming, and that the answer is steadfast loyalty. They are given one comfort in verse 8: their names are written in the Lamb's book, and the beast's reach does not extend to that.

And he meant them to think. 'Here is a call for wisdom' is addressed to readers who must discern when the state's claims have crossed a line. The first hearers were not asked to wait for a distant figure; they were asked to recognize the beastly pattern in their own empire, and to refuse its worship while still praying for those in authority. The chapter equips the church for the long pressure of a world that offers comfort for compromise.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what the dragon's agents do and what God allows. It does not command believers to hate the state, and it should not be set against Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2, which call for respect for rulers. The two fit together: a government that keeps order serves God, and a government that demands worship has become the beast. The task is to tell the difference and to give to Caesar what is Caesar's without giving him what is God's, Mark 12:17.

The chapter also does not authorize date-setting or the naming of modern figures as the beast. Every generation has identified its enemy with the beast, and each has been wrong about the final form while sometimes right about the pattern. What the chapter commands is endurance and discernment. The warning about captivity and the sword, verse 10, is a description of what the faithful should expect, and a call to hold on, not a command to inflict the same on others. Believers apply it by refusing idolatry in whatever form it takes, by counting the cost of loyalty, and by resting in the promise that those written in the Lamb's book belong to Him.

debates.question: Who or what is the beast from the sea, and what does 666 mean?

views.label: A first-century emperor, Nero or Domitian, and the cult of Rome
views.case: Read in its own setting, the beast combines Daniel's four beasts into the Roman empire, whose emperors demanded divine honors. The healed mortal wound may recall the legend that Nero would return from death, and in Hebrew gematria the letters of 'Nero Caesar' sum to 666, with some early manuscripts reading 616, matching a Latinized spelling of the same name, so John's first hearers could plausibly have recognized their own persecutor.

views.label: A future end-time ruler, or a timeless pattern in every beastly regime
views.case: Because the vision's universal worship, economic control, and warfare against the saints outstrip anything Nero or Domitian actually achieved, many read the beast as a still-future individual who will revive and perfect the dragon's programme, while others read it as a recurring pattern embodied differently by every generation's God-defying power, with 666 marking a persistent, threefold falling short of God's completeness, pictured by the number seven.

debates.bearing: Whichever referent is primarily in view, the passage's force does not depend on solving the puzzle. The beast is real, blasphemous, and demands what belongs to God alone, and every generation must discern its counterfeit worship and refuse it.

debates.question: Is the mark of the beast a specific, literal mark, or a symbol of total allegiance?

views.label: A literal, identifiable mark
views.case: The text is specific about hand and forehead and about buying and selling, paralleling real ancient practices of stamped certificates for trade and branding of soldiers and slaves, so many futurist readers expect a literal, identifiable mark still to come, perhaps tied to future technology.

views.label: A symbol of total economic and religious conformity
views.case: The mark parodies God's own seal placed on the foreheads of His servants in chapter 7, so the point is allegiance made visible in the ordinary transactions of daily life rather than one specific technology. On this reading the mark names whatever system forces a person's livelihood into open allegiance to the beast.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that the mark represents a real, costly choice between visible allegiance to the beast's system and joining the Lamb's marked, persevering people, whatever concrete form that choice takes in a given generation.

study.originalLanguages:
The word therion, 'beast,' is used for wild animals, in contrast to the domestic ones. It is the same word the Septuagint uses for Daniel's four beasts. It first appears in Revelation 11:7 for the one that comes up from the Abyss, and the sea beast of chapter 13 is that same figure, now described in full. The earth beast has no separate name here, but it is the same one called the false prophet in Revelation 19:20.

In verse 3 the head is 'mortally wounded,' with the Greek esphagmenen eis thanaton, 'slain to death.' The verb sphazo, to slaughter, is the one John uses for the Lamb 'as though slain' in Revelation 5:6, and the two descriptions are almost identical in wording. The healing of the wound is therefore an imitation of the Lamb's resurrection. In verse 4 the crowd asks, 'Who is like the beast?' The question parodies the praise of Exodus 15:11, 'Who is like You, O LORD?', and perhaps the name Michael, which means 'Who is like God?' and appears in the previous chapter.

The word 'blasphemous' in verses 1, 5, and 6 is blasphemia, and what the beast speaks is directed against God's name and His tabernacle, verse 6. The verb skenoo, 'to dwell as in a tent,' used in 12:12 for those who dwell in heaven, is related to the word for 'tabernacle' here, so the beast slanders the dwelling of God and those who dwell with Him.

A well known ambiguity occurs in verse 8. The Greek can be read as names written 'from the foundation of the world' in the book of life, or as the Lamb slain 'from the foundation of the world.' The BSB takes the first and notes the second. Revelation 17:8 supports the first reading, since it speaks of names not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world.

In verse 11 the second beast has two horns like a lamb, arnion, the same diminutive John uses for Christ throughout the book. The verb for the image's 'breath' in verse 15 is pneuma, which also means spirit, and the image receives it from the beast, in a distant parody of Genesis 2:7.

The mark is charagma, an engraved or stamped sign, and in Acts 17:29 the same word is used for an idol 'formed by man's design.' The mark comes with a name or a number, and verse 18 says the number is 'of a man,' arithmos anthropou, which may mean a human number or the number of a particular man. The sword saying of verse 10 is drawn from Jeremiah 15:2, as the BSB footnote notes, and some manuscripts differ on whether it speaks of being killed or of killing.

typology.fulfillment: Daniel saw four beasts rise from the sea, each a kingdom, and the fourth had ten horns. John sees one beast that carries the features of the first three and the horns of the fourth, so every proud power of history is gathered into one pattern. The correspondence shows that the empires Daniel foresaw were not unrelated. In Christ the pattern is judged: the Ancient of Days takes His seat, the beast is slain, and the kingdom goes to the Son of Man, Daniel 7:9 to 14. The type falls short because Daniel's beasts are successive, while John's is the summing up.

A king set up an image and decreed that all must worship it or die, and three faithful men refused. The earth beast makes an image of the sea beast, gives it breath, and has those who refuse killed. The correspondence offers a pattern for the saints: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego said that God could rescue them, 'but even if He does not,' they would not bow, Daniel 3:17 to 18. Christ is the true image of God, Colossians 1:15, and believers are being conformed to Him, Romans 8:29. The type falls short because the three emerged from the fire, while many in Revelation do not.

typology.type: The counterfeit Lamb and the false seal
typology.fulfillment: The beast's wound that was healed imitates the Lamb that was slain and lives, and its mark counterfeits the seal of God on the foreheads of His servants, Revelation 7:3. The beast's worshipers say 'Who is like the beast?' in imitation of Israel's praise of God. Each feature is a counterfeit, and the original is Christ: His resurrection, His sealing, His worthiness. The correspondence is by contrast, not likeness. The fake always falls short, because it cannot give life, and the Lamb's book of life stands against the beast's mark.

typology.type: Pharaoh and his control of the people's labor
typology.fulfillment: Pharaoh forced Israel to build and tried to control their work and worship, Exodus 1 and 5. The second beast controls who can buy and sell and demands allegiance in the marketplace. The pattern is oppression through economic dependence. The answer in both cases is the Lord's rescue: He heard their groaning and brought them out, Exodus 2:24 and 12:51. In Christ the deliverance is complete, since He has freed His people to serve God, Luke 1:74. The type falls short because Israel's rescue was geographical, while the church's is from the dominion of darkness, Colossians 1:13.

study.christ:
Revelation 13 reaches Christ almost entirely by contrast, and the contrasts are sharp. The beast has a head 'slain to death' and healed, and the Lamb was slain and lives, Revelation 5:6 and 1:18. The beast receives the dragon's power, throne, and authority, and the Son received all authority in heaven and earth from the Father, Matthew 28:18, after refusing the very offer the dragon makes in Matthew 4:8 to 10, where the devil showed Him all the kingdoms and promised them for one act of worship. The beast demands worship through force and wonders, while Christ gained the worship of the redeemed by laying down His life, Revelation 5:9 to 10.

The beast makes war on the saints and conquers them, verse 7, and Christ also was put to death by the powers of His day. The difference is that His death was the means of His victory, and when the beast 'conquers' the saints it does so only within what God permits, and they too overcome by the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 12:11. The beast seems to win in the very hour of its defeat, which is the pattern of the cross.

The Lamb's book of life appears in verse 8, and the Lamb is called 'the Lamb who was slain,' which ties the believer's security to His death. Whichever way the Greek is read, whether names written from the foundation of the world or the Lamb slain from that time, the book belongs to Him and the names are in His keeping. Jesus told the disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven, Luke 10:20.

The earth beast has two horns like a lamb. The lamb is the symbol of Christ, and this creature uses the look of gentleness to carry the dragon's voice. Jesus warned of wolves in sheep's clothing, Matthew 7:15, and of false christs and false prophets with great signs, Matthew 24:24. The way to tell the true from the false is by the message: the true Lamb points to God, and the false lamb points to the beast.

The chapter's gift is to prepare the church to prize Christ. Anyone who has seen how the counterfeit works learns to look for the real thing: the one who bears scars, who does not coerce, and who is the faithful witness. Take care not to build a doctrine of Christ out of the number 666 or the details of the mark. The links are the New Testament's own: the slain Lamb, the true image of God, and the book of life He holds.
study.god:
This is a chapter about evil, and its first lesson about God is that He is not threatened by it. The beast has a mouth to speak, authority to act for 42 months, and permission to wage war, and every one of these is given. The repeated passive, 'was given,' hides God as the one who gives, the way the Bible often speaks. The beast is on a leash. Job 1:12 and 2:6 show the same pattern with Satan, and Luke 22:31 shows Satan asking permission to sift Peter. The God who is sovereign over evil is not its author, and the text does not explain how both can be true. It states each and asks for trust.

He is a God who knows His own. The book of life belongs to the Lamb, and names there were written 'from the foundation of the world,' which means that no one who belongs to Him can be taken. The beast gets worshipers, but it cannot touch the list. This gives the assurance of Romans 8:38 to 39, that nothing can separate believers from the love of God.

He is also the one who calls for endurance. The call for 'perseverance and faith' shows that God does not promise exemption from suffering but gives strength in it. He is the God who walked with Daniel's friends in the fire, Daniel 3:25, and is present with His church in the pressure of the beast.

The chapter shows God's holiness in what the beast lacks and what it steals. Worship belongs to God alone, and every attempt to take it is blasphemy, a word the text uses repeatedly. The first commandment, Exodus 20:3, is the real issue behind the mark and the image. The God who is jealous for His own name is the same God who sets limits on those who seek to usurp it.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to give all ultimate loyalty to God and to look past the glamour of the world's power. It teaches us to trust His timing, since forty-two months is a number the dragon cannot extend, and to find our security not in avoiding the beast's attention but in the Lamb's book. A church that knows whose it is can face the beast without bowing.

crossReferences.note: Daniel's four beasts rise from the sea, and the fourth has ten horns and a mouth speaking great boasts. Revelation 13:1 to 2 combines them, listing the leopard, bear, and lion, and gives the beast the horns and the mouth of the final one.

The horn speaks words against the Most High, wears down the holy ones, and is given power for a time, times, and half a time. The beast's blasphemy, war with the saints, and 42 months in verses 5 to 7 are drawn from this verse, and the limit is the same: a time that God sets.

Nebuchadnezzar sets up a gold image and requires everyone to worship it on pain of death. The second beast's image in verses 14 and 15 repeats the pattern of an empire demanding worship under penalty of death, and the three friends who refused are the model for the saints.

Israel sings, 'Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?' after the sea closes over Pharaoh. The crowd's question, 'Who is like the beast?', in Revelation 13:4 turns the song of the redeemed into praise of the usurper.

The Lord tells Jeremiah that some are destined for death, some for the sword, some for captivity. Revelation 13:10 draws on it, as the BSB footnote notes, to say that the saints must expect captivity and the sword, and that endurance is the proper reply.

Paul speaks of the man of lawlessness who exalts himself, takes his seat in God's temple, and comes with the work of Satan in counterfeit signs and wonders. The beasts of Revelation 13 are the fuller picture of this deceiving power and of the people who perish because they refuse the truth.

An angel seals the servants of God on their foreheads. The mark of the beast on hand or forehead is the counterfeit of this seal, so the chapter presents two competing claims of ownership, and each person bears one.

The beast that was, is not, and is about to come up from the Abyss, and those whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel. It supports reading Revelation 13:8 as names written from the foundation of the world.

Paul tells believers to submit to governing authorities, since God has established them. It must be read with Revelation 13: the same state that serves God by restraining evil becomes the beast when it demands worship. The two passages together describe what a Christian owes and what a Christian must refuse.

Jesus warns that false christs and false prophets will perform great signs and wonders to mislead, if possible, even the elect. The signs of the second beast, verses 13 and 14, are the fulfillment of this warning, and Jesus' 'See, I have told you in advance' is the reason the church does not need to be surprised.

study.oneStory:
The Bible is the story of a king and a counterfeit. From the garden onward the serpent offers a shortcut to godhood, and every empire that follows repeats the offer in political form. Pharaoh claimed the Nile, Nebuchadnezzar set up his image, and Antiochus Epiphanes desecrated the temple. Each was a preview, and Daniel gathered them into beasts that would be judged. Revelation 13 brings that long record to a point: the final shape of the dragon's counterfeit kingdom.

The chapter answers a question from the end of chapter 12. If the dragon has been thrown down and cannot reach the woman, how does he make war on the rest of her children? He works through the powers of this world, the political and the religious, the one with force and the other with persuasion. The sea beast and earth beast are not new inventions but the age-old combination of the sword and the lie.

Its place in the story is also to define the choice. In the garden the choice was between God's word and the serpent's. Here it is between the Lamb's book and the beast's mark, between worshipping the Creator and worshipping the creature, Romans 1:25. The saints are called to endure, and their endurance is itself a kind of testimony, as the story of Daniel's friends has shown.

The story moves on to its judgment. In Revelation 19:20 the beast is captured and the false prophet with it, and they are thrown into the lake of fire. The dragon follows in 20:10. And in the new creation, the nations walk by the light of the Lamb, and nothing unclean will ever enter it, but only those whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life, Revelation 21:27. The counterfeit is ended, and the true King reigns.

sermon.title: The Beast, the Book, and the Beauty of the Lamb
sermon.why: Piper expounds Revelation 13:1-10 directly, centering on the Book of Life of the slain Lamb as the reason believers will not worship the beast, which is exactly the turn this study makes from the beast's counterfeit power to the security found only in Christ.

quiz.q: What does the beast from the sea receive from the dragon?

options.text: The dragon's own power, throne, and great authority.
options.note: Revelation 13:2 states the dragon gave the beast his power, throne, and authority.

options.text: Only a temporary alliance with no shared authority.
options.note: The text is stronger than an alliance; the dragon directly transfers his power and throne.

options.text: A crown taken from the Lamb.
options.note: The beast's authority comes from the dragon, not from the Lamb.

options.text: Nothing; the beast acts entirely on its own.
options.note: The beast is explicitly empowered by the dragon, not self-sufficient.

quiz.q: Whose names are protected from worshiping the beast?

options.text: Those written from the foundation of the world in the Lamb's Book of Life.
options.note: Revelation 13:8 names this as the deciding factor.

options.text: Anyone who is politically powerful enough to resist.
options.note: The protection is not political strength but being written in the Lamb's book.

options.text: Only the twelve apostles.
options.note: The promise is for all whose names are in the Book of Life, not a fixed small group.

options.text: No one; all people without exception worship the beast.
options.note: The text explicitly excepts those written in the Book of Life.

quiz.q: What is the role of the second beast, from the earth?

options.text: It performs deceptive signs and forces worship of the first beast, including through an image that speaks.
options.note: Revelation 13:12-15 describes this false-prophet role.

options.text: It replaces the first beast as the main ruler.
options.note: It serves and promotes the first beast rather than replacing it.

options.text: It fights against the first beast to protect the saints.
options.note: It works for the first beast, enforcing worship of it, not opposing it.

options.text: It has no connection to the first beast.
options.note: It exists specifically to exercise the first beast's authority and compel its worship.

quiz.q: What does the mark of the beast control?

options.text: The ability to buy or sell in the ordinary business of daily life.
options.note: Revelation 13:17 ties the mark directly to commerce.

options.text: Only entrance into pagan temples.
options.note: The text specifies buying and selling, a broader, everyday reach than temple access.

options.text: Access to military service only.
options.note: The mark's stated purpose is economic, not military.

options.text: Nothing of practical consequence.
options.note: The mark has real, everyday economic consequences for those without it.

quiz.q: What response does the chapter call for in the face of the beast's authority?

options.text: Perseverance and faith, discerned with wisdom, not violent resistance.
options.note: Revelation 13:10 and 18 call for endurance, faith, and wisdom.

options.text: Immediate armed rebellion against the beast's forces.
options.note: The call is to endurance and faith, not armed revolt.

options.text: Silent agreement with whatever the beast demands.
options.note: The saints are called to refuse the beast's worship, not comply silently.

options.text: No response is called for at all.
options.note: The chapter explicitly calls for perseverance, faith, and wisdom.

questions: The beast controlled who could buy or sell. Where do you feel pressure today to compromise your convictions for the sake of financial or social security?
The whole world marveled at the beast's healed wound and followed it. What counterfeit forms of power or salvation are tempting to admire and follow in your own life right now?

The saints were called to perseverance and faith rather than fear or fighting on the world's terms. What would it look like this week to endure faithfully in a hard situation rather than escape it or compromise?
Only those written in the Lamb's Book of Life were kept from worshiping the beast. How does resting in that security, rather than in your own strength, change the way you face pressure to conform?

The chapter calls for wisdom to discern the beast's true nature rather than being deceived by its signs. Where do you need to ask God for discernment about a power, system, or trend that claims more allegiance than it deserves?

translationNotes.note: The 42 months is the same limited span found elsewhere in Revelation as 1,260 days or a time, times, and half a time, echoing Daniel 7:25 and 12:7; it marks a real but God-limited period of persecution, not an unbounded reign.

The Greek word order allows 'from the foundation of the world' to modify either 'written' (names written down from the foundation of the world) or 'slain' (the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, as in some translations of Revelation 13:8 and the parallel in 17:8). Both readings are true to the rest of Scripture, and translators differ.

Some early manuscripts, including Papyrus 115, read 616 instead of 666. Both numbers have been connected historically to the gematria value of 'Nero Caesar' spelled different ways, though the text itself calls it simply 'the number of a man.'
The beast's composite features, a leopard's body, a bear's feet, and a lion's mouth, are drawn directly from the four separate beasts of Daniel 7:4-6, now combined into a single final power.
